planting.note: Set out container plants or rooted semi-hardwood cuttings in fall or spring in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun; this naturally occurring hybrid between Cistus populifolius and Cistus salviifolius is one of the more cold-tolerant rockroses.

directions: Plant in lean, fast-draining, alkaline-to-neutral soil in full sun, giving the wide-spreading mound room to fill in without crowding. Cistus x hybridus bears a long late-spring to early-summer succession of crinkled, 2-inch white flowers with a bright yellow-anthered center against wavy, gray-green, sage-scented leaves, and it holds its foliage evergreen through mild winters. It is notably more cold-hardy and adaptable than many named rockrose cultivars, tolerating light frost and poor rocky soil, but still resents wet feet and heavy clay. Shear lightly right after flowering to keep the mound dense, since old wood seldom resprouts if cut back hard.

planting.note: Set out container plants or root semi-hardwood cuttings in fall or spring in lean, gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun; grey-leaved rockrose is one of the most drought-tolerant Cistus once established.

directions: Site in lean, fast-draining, alkaline soil in full sun; Cistus albidus forms a rounded, felted mound of soft gray-white leaves that contrast handsomely with clusters of 2 to 3-inch rose-pink to rose-purple flowers carried through late spring and into summer. The dense woolly hairs on the foliage give the plant excellent heat and glare tolerance, making it a strong choice for reflected-heat sites, gravel gardens, and slopes where irrigation is scarce. As with other rockroses, avoid rich soil, mulch piled against the crown, and summer watering once the plant is established, and skip hard pruning into bare wood since old growth resprouts poorly.

planting.note: Set out container plants or root semi-hardwood cuttings in fall or spring in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun; this is generally regarded as the most cold-hardy of the rockroses.

directions: Plant in lean, fast-draining, neutral-to-alkaline soil in full sun, allowing plenty of room for this larger, upright rockrose to develop into a substantial rounded shrub. Cistus laurifolius carries leathery, dark green, laurel-like leaves that are strongly aromatic and resinous, and in early to midsummer it is covered in 2 to 3-inch white flowers marked with a yellow blotch at the base of each petal. Along with Cistus ladanifer, this species is a traditional source of labdanum resin, and its resinous foliage helps it shrug off heat, drought, and poor rocky soil once established. It tolerates more cold than most Cistus but, like its relatives, will not survive winter wet or heavy clay.

planting.note: Set out container plants or root semi-hardwood cuttings in fall or spring in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun; named selections such as Silver Pink are propagated only from cuttings, never seed.

directions: Grow in lean, fast-draining, alkaline-to-neutral soil in full sun. 'Silver Pink' is a compact hybrid rockrose prized for its clear silvery-pink, 2 to 3-inch flowers with crumpled petals and a boss of golden stamens, set against narrow, gray-green, resinous leaves. It flowers heavily over several weeks in early summer and, like other Cistus hybrids, is more free-flowering and slightly more cold-hardy than many straight species. Keep the root zone lean and dry, avoid mulching against the crown, and shear lightly right after bloom to maintain a tidy mound, since old wood rarely resprouts if cut back hard.

common_name: Lambrook Silver Cotton Lavender (Fine-Leaved Gray Santolina)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; named cultivars such as Lambrook Silver are propagated from cuttings rather than seed.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; this selection needs the same superb drainage as the species and will rot in wet or humid, poorly aerated soil. 'Lambrook Silver' is a widely grown cultivar selected for finer, more feathery, more intensely silver-white foliage than the species, giving it a softer, lacier texture that is especially prized in knot gardens and silver borders. It produces the same small, bright-yellow, button-like flower heads in midsummer, though many gardeners shear the flower buds off to keep the foliage effect uninterrupted. Trim after flowering (or in place of flowering) to maintain a dense, rounded habit and prevent the center from opening up and becoming woody.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in lean, gravelly or sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; named selections are grown from cuttings rather than seed.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in lean, gravelly or sandy, well-drained soil in full sun. Spanish gorse forms a dense, low, intensely spiny mound of dark green stems that disappears beneath a heavy flush of small, bright golden-yellow, pea-shaped flowers in late spring and early summer, followed by good repeat bloom into summer. The formidable spines make it a useful barrier or slope-stabilizing plant as well as an ornamental, and its tight habit needs no shearing to stay tidy. As with other brooms, good drainage is essential; it declines quickly in heavy or waterlogged soil but shrugs off heat, poor fertility, and drought once established.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in lean, gravelly or sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; this named selection is grown from cuttings rather than seed.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in lean, gravelly or sandy, well-drained soil in full sun. 'Vancouver Gold' is a ground-hugging, mat-forming broom that spreads wider than it is tall, its trailing stems studded with small silky-haired leaves and smothered in bright golden-yellow, pea-shaped flowers for several weeks in late spring. It is exceptionally useful for cascading over rock walls, covering dry banks, or filling gaps between paving in a gravel garden, and it tolerates poor, lean soil far better than rich, moist beds. Good drainage is essential year-round, and once established it needs almost no supplemental water or fertilizer.

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring, since brooms resent root disturbance and transplant poorly once established; choose the final site carefully in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun.

directions: Set out young, container-grown plants in spring in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun, choosing the permanent site with care since Mount Etna broom resents being moved once established. Native to the volcanic slopes of Sicily and Sardinia, it develops into a large, airy, weeping small tree with fine, nearly leafless, rush-like green stems that cast light, dappled shade, and it is smothered in small, fragrant, golden-yellow pea flowers in mid to late summer, later than most brooms. Its graceful, almost willow-like silhouette and tolerance of poor, rocky, infertile soil make it a striking specimen or light-canopy tree for a dry garden. It needs no irrigation once rooted in and should never be cut back hard into bare wood, which brooms will not resprout from.

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring in lean, fast-draining, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; brooms resent root disturbance, so choose the final site carefully rather than planning to move it later.

directions: Set out container-grown plants in spring in lean, fast-draining, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun. 'Allgold' is a deep golden-flowered selection of the Warminster broom hybrid, its slender arching stems wreathed in small pea-shaped flowers for several weeks in mid to late spring, ahead of most other brooms. The fine, nearly leafless green stems keep the shrub looking fresh through the growing season and give it a graceful, fountain-like form. Avoid rich or heavily amended soil and skip hard pruning into old wood, which brooms rarely resprout from; instead, shear lightly right after flowering to keep the plant dense and prevent it from becoming leggy and open at the base.

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring in lean to average, fast-draining soil in full sun; in colder parts of its range it benefits from the shelter and reflected heat of a south- or west-facing wall.

directions: Set out container-grown plants in spring in lean to average, fast-draining soil in full sun, ideally with the shelter of a warm wall in cooler climates. Unlike most brooms, pineapple broom carries distinctive silvery, silky-haired, trifoliate leaves reminiscent of a laburnum, and in summer it produces dense, upright, cone-shaped racemes of bright yellow flowers with a strong, unmistakable pineapple fragrance. It grows quickly into a large, loose, open shrub or small multi-stemmed tree and tolerates poor, rocky soil and drought once established, though it appreciates a sunny, sheltered spot away from harsh winter wind. Prune lightly after flowering only if needed to shape, since it does not resprout reliably from old bare wood.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; this low, spreading broom is more shade-tolerant than most of its relatives.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade. Purple broom is a low, mounding to sprawling shrublet, unusual among brooms both for its lilac-purple, pea-shaped flowers in late spring and for its willingness to flower well with some afternoon shade, making it a useful edging or rock-garden broom for sites that get less than full sun. Its fine green stems stay tidy without shearing, and it tolerates poor, rocky soil far better than fertile, regularly watered beds. Avoid heavy or waterlogged soil, and skip hard pruning into old wood, which brooms rarely resprout from.
scientific_name_note: Also classified as Chamaecytisus purpureus by some taxonomic authorities; widely sold under the name Cytisus purpureus.

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun; Spanish broom resents root disturbance, so choose the permanent site carefully.

directions: Set out container-grown plants in spring in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun, giving the shrub room to develop its loose, upright, broom-like form. Spartium junceum is the sole species in its genus, distinguished by rounded, rush-like, nearly leafless blue-green stems that carry out most of the plant's photosynthesis, topped from late spring through summer by a long succession of large, intensely fragrant, golden-yellow pea flowers. It is extremely tolerant of heat, drought, wind, poor rocky soil, and seaside salt spray, and needs no irrigation or fertilizer once established, but it can self-sow readily and has naturalized in some mild, dry regions, so spent flowers can be deadheaded where volunteer seedlings are unwanted. Avoid hard pruning into bare wood, which the plant does not reliably resprout from.
